coherence.reasons: X's hierarchy is very tight: the governing thought carries both the answer and its binding condition (Amazon-led, pays back only below 28.6% ACoS), four arguments each have two supporting facts, and the sections map one-to-one onto those arguments. Y is also well structured, but looser. Its 'Risks and ambition' section merges two different arguments. The slide 4 title ('$40M would need only about 1% of it') sits awkwardly with the later conclusion that no route reaches $40M. Its headline ranges also drift: peak cash is given as -$1.9M to -$3.9M alongside a '$6.4M worst tested case', and the Option A margin floor appears as 9.0%, 9.1% and 8.8% in different places. The Japan trade-off line also mixes a gross figure ($1.8M forgone) with a net one ($4.1M). X is more internally consistent, though the gap is small.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred recommendation (Amazon-led with gates, reject retail-led, Japan as the alternative, reset the ambition) and compare the options on the board's own constraints. Y weighs the trade-offs more fully. It puts the ambition-versus-guardrails choice to the board as an explicit decision, with the alternative (relax the guardrails) costed and rejected. It models volume risk as well as ad cost: a stall case anchored on the two Amazon-first peers below $5M, and a 20%-below-plan case. Its gates have tiered if-missed responses (hold ad growth, scale back, or exit, with the cash at stake), plus a second gate at end-2028 and a $4M envelope. Its retail trigger requires a right-sized plan that fits the guardrails, not just awareness. X is sound and adds a sharp insight Y lacks: Japan returns more cash above 25.9% ACoS, an honest admission that Japan wins on cash at the pilot's ad cost. But X tests no volume downside, and its go/no-go gate compares a first-year reading with a four-year average threshold, which it concedes a costly first year could offset. X's treatment of the ambition is an assertion ('read it as about $26M'), not a weighed choice.

evidence.reasons: The two models agree with each other and with the key on every core figure: Option A at +$2.40M / +$0.38M / -$2.32M for 25% / 28% / 32% ACoS, break-even at 28.6% (26.9% with the tariff), Option B peak at -$20.8M, and group margin of 4.5% in 2027. Y shows more of the required working: pre-ad contribution of $10.73, post-ad at all three ACoS levels, retail contribution of $7.55, and CAGR of 17.3% against 5.1%. Y also uses the critical evidence more deeply. It notes that even the upper quartile (3.4) in Onsoo's awareness band is below the 4.0 delisting bar. Its sell-through-by-halo grid shows Option B fails structurally in every cell. It calculates how much US loss the margin floor can absorb. Y does carry a few weaker inferences: the '$40M is about 1% of the market' headline is close to market-share sizing, the 333k-unit figure is a linear extrapolation of the pilot, and the 2032 date rests on an assumed 23% growth rate. Y flags the last two as a trend held flat and as illustrative, and neither drives the recommendation. X is cleaner on unsupported claims: it uses the conservative June run-rate and adds the Japan break-even calculation. But it leaves retail unit economics implicit, gives no CAGR, and asserts that Amazon fees are 'fixed by contract' without support. Both handle the correlation memo, the $5.2B figure and the competitor histories correctly.

revision.reasons: Both keep the CEO's Amazon-first launch and add conditions, as the evidence warrants. Both also correct the 15% awareness trigger: brands at 10-20% awareness sell 3.5 units per door per week, below the 4.0 bar. And both model the CEO's 2029 national-retail step to show it breaks payback and the margin floor. Y is more explicit and complete. It breaks the hypothesis into seven testable conditions with a verdict on each (holds, at risk, fails) and states a revised answer. It replaces the trigger with awareness above 20%, Amazon revenue of at least $20M and a plan that fits the guardrails. It tests the 2029 step at the more realistic 28% ACoS, and both with and without the halo. It makes re-phasing the $40M ambition a formal board decision. X reaches the same substantive updates, but keeps the CEO's $10M Amazon threshold unexamined and resets the ambition only by reinterpretation.

overall.reasons: Both documents are strong and avoid the main traps. Each rejects retail-led on the cap, payback and margin floor, tests the 25% ACoS and 4.5 units-per-door assumptions against the benchmarks, identifies the 28.6% break-even, and concludes that $40M is not reachable within the constraints. X is the more economical and tightly argued, and its Japan break-even ACoS is a useful insight. Y would serve the board better because it turns the same analysis into decisions. It sets out five explicit approvals, puts the ambition-versus-guardrails choice squarely to the board, and sizes a funding envelope. Its gates say what happens if they are missed, and it tests volume and stall downsides as well as ad cost. It also audits the CEO's hypothesis condition by condition. Y's weaknesses are a market-share headline and two flagged extrapolations, none of which drives the recommendation.
